abstract: Scientific-literature discovery combines evidence acquisition with decisions about when a search may stop. These functions are often evaluated as one policy, although a locally exhausted or unavailable route does not establish that the scientific task is complete. We introduce a fail-closed control layer that separates route stopping from task closure, screens route distinctness by provenance, distinguishes content identity from question-conditioned processing, and retains unresolved material routes as open obligations. A 390-task complete-gold index supplies descriptive mechanism evidence: mean recall is 0.979487 with no premature task closure, but the study does not establish superiority. In a 400-case exact-contract battery, the controller matches all 400 declared labels, compared with 250 for an authored comparator assembled from prior mechanisms but excluding unavailable material routes. An information-equivalent comparator also matches 400, bounding the claim to the closure contract. A descriptive TREC-COVID comparison is adverse on recall and cost. Against BM25, recall@100 is lower by 0.01769, with a 95% bootstrap interval of [-0.02729,-0.00906], and reads increase by 175.7%. Although nDCG@10 is higher by 0.1488, the opposing results do not establish overall superiority. Density-normalized and query-conditional BEIR successors leave all five ArguAna decisions unchanged. These transformations are decision-inert under the tested rule. The contribution is therefore a bounded control method, not evidence of external retrieval superiority or open-world completeness.
comments: 21 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables; adverse, favorable, null, undetermined, and unaccessed results retained
title: Acquisition Is Not Closure: Fail-Closed Control for Open-World Scientific-Literature Discovery
